#139436. Is trust in science falling, or does it just feel that way?

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1924 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nature ↗ Open Full Page

Is trust in science falling, or does it just feel that way?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1924 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that this article is the third in a series discussing the results of Nature’s 2026 science-job satisfaction survey.
  • Iris Borowy thinks that teaching her postgraduate students how to tell fact from fiction is central to her job.
  • Industry observers note that borowy is one of the researchers who told a Nature survey earlier this year that they felt public trust in science had declined over the previous five years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Illustration: Gheleyne Bastiaen.

Industry observers note that this article is the third in a series discussing the results of Nature’s 2026 science-job satisfaction survey. It’s the latest edition of such surveys, which started in 2010; the last two took place in 2018 and 2021. The 2026 survey, created in partnership with Thinks Insight & Strategy, a research consultancy in London, introduced in May and was advertised on nature.com, in Springer Nature digital products and through e-mail campaigns. It had 3,882 self-selecting respondents across 133 countries with 31% describing themselves as female and 19% as belonging to a minority ethnic group in their country of work. The full survey data sets are available at go.nature.com/4b2drrc.

Iris Borowy thinks that teaching her postgraduate students how to tell fact from fiction is central to her job. Yet some days, that work seems futile. “I feel silly teaching groups of eight people while, out there in the influencer sphere, complete idiots talk to millions,” says Borowy, a global-development historian at Shanghai University in China. “Granted, there are a lot of serious people doing good work online, but working against the propaganda is getting harder.”.

Industry observers note that borowy is one of the researchers who told a Nature survey earlier this year that they felt public trust in science had declined over the previous five years. Of around 3,900 respondents, 50% shared this view, with 33% thinking that trust had increased and 13% saying that it had stayed the same (see ‘Perceptions versus reality of public trust in science’).

It has been revealed that even though trust in science remains high overall, data from other surveys support the idea that trust levels have fallen slightly, after rising at the start of the COVID-19 pandemic. A global survey of more than 140,000 people in 140 nations, published in October by the London-based funding charity Wellcome, found that the proportion of the public who trust science “a lot” or “some” declined from 80% in 2020 to 72% in 2025. Trust levels dropped below pre-pandemic levels in 5 of 14 regions: Australia and Latest Zealand, sub-Saharan Africa and central, western and eastern Asia. It rose in just two areas — western and southern Europe. In seven regions, including North America and northern Europe, it remained close to the 2018 pre-pandemic levels, when 77% of overall respondents expressed trust in science.

It has been revealed that nature’s survey data — which measure scientists’ perceptions of changes in public trust levels, not trust levels themselves — only partly match the trends in the Wellcome survey. In our self-selecting survey, respondents in Africa and Asia were the least likely to say that trust in science had dropped (28% and 34%, respectively). By contrast, 78% of respondents in North America and 64% in Europe thought that public trust had declined. Nature’s survey also revealed that perceptions of falling public trust colour scientists’ job satisfaction and influence who they think is ultimately responsible for rebuilding trust.

How the pandemic changed trust in science — in four charts.

How the pandemic changed trust in science — in four charts.

It has been revealed that the mismatch between actual trust levels in North America and Europe, which remain relatively high, and some scientists’ impression that they’re markedly declining could be explained by a few things, states Niels Mede, a science-communication researcher at Wageningen University in the Netherlands. One is that people who don’t trust science have become louder and more visible, particularly online, and that their messaging is making scientists feel threatened. This has driven a narrative in science media and policy debates of a “crisis of trust”, he says, which has fuelled the perception that overall trust is going down. In addition, he says, many scientists hold a pessimistic view of the public — seeing lay audiences as uninterested in and apathetic to science.

There is also strong evidence that, in countries where scientists told Nature they felt trust in science had dropped, opinions about science are becoming more polarized along political lines. This is especially visible in the United States, where trust among right-leaning Republicans dropped sharply after the COVID-19 pandemic, whereas trust among left-leaning Democrats remained high. In the Netherlands, trust in science remains high overall but the proportion expressing low trust grew from 9.5% in 2019 to 14.6% in 2025. A UK survey published in April found that the proportion who trusted science “a lot” had dropped from 63% in 2020 to just 34%.

Given the gap between perceptions and realities when it comes to public trust of science, Mede notes that it’s important to read the trends in Nature’s survey “as a measure of how scientists experience their relationship with the public, not as a measure of public trust per se”.

Digging down into the country-level data from the Nature survey, it is clear that there are big geographical differences in scientists’ perceptions of public trust.

In the United States, 83% of respondents felt that trust in science had decreased in the past five years, compared with 79% in Germany and 78% in the United Kingdom. By contrast, just 23% of respondents in India reported feeling that public trust in science had decreased, with a considerable majority — 61% — saying that they felt it had increased. In Japan, 37% of respondents felt trust in science has decreased, whereas 38% mentioned it has stayed the same.

Sources indicate that what’s the secret sauce for happy scientists at work? These eight countries offer some clues.

What’s the secret sauce for happy scientists at work? These eight countries offer some clues.

Nature’s findings from respondents in India closely match national data on public trust in science. In a survey across 68 countries published last year, India was the country with the second-highest trust in scientists after Egypt. Mede, who was one of the study’s authors, thinks that strong pro-science rhetoric from the Indian government could play a part in the country’s high trust levels.

The Indian constitution even lists developing a “scientific temper” — meaning one that is led by logic and evidence instead of belief or superstition — among the duties of its citizens. Mede claims that Indian scientists might view this pro-science political climate as a proxy for public trust.

Sources indicate that nature’s survey data for Japan suggests that scientists there feel that public trust is relatively stable, even if the actual level of trust might be modest, says Sotaro Shibayama, an economist of science at the University of Tokyo. This makes sense to him, because he thinks that science is less politicized in his country than it is in nations where a higher proportion felt trust had dropped. Studies indicate that trust in science fluctuates in Japan as well, Shibayama says, “but these fluctuations may be smaller than in countries where science has become more closely entangled with political and ideological divisions”.

When asked what is driving the falling levels of trust, the responses indicate that scientists view distrust more as a problem originating externally, rather than something caused from within. Some 69% said that misinformation was the main cause, followed by political pressure or influence on science (62%) and a lack of public understanding of science (54%). Survey-takers could select more than one driver and this question was asked only of those who answered that trust had declined.

Only 24% thought that increased scrutiny and scepticism of experts was a main driver of falling trust and just 23% thought that scientists’ communication with the public was to blame. “We often do not have training in science communication, nor do we really need it,” wrote one early-career Earth and atmospheric scientist in Portugal. “We are paid, and should be paid, to do science.”.

Have people stopped trusting science? The data tell a surprising story.

Have people stopped trusting science? The data tell a surprising story.

But Mede indicates that the evidence that misinformation and a lack of public understanding erode trust significantly is “much thinner and more mixed than one would expect”. Shared values and transparency might matter more. A UK study published in September found that trust was shaped less by whether the public viewed scientists as experts and more by whether scientists were ‘on their side’. Perceptions of openness and transparency also mattered for trust, the study found: 73% of those with high trust in scientists agreed that scientists were generally open and transparent, compared with just 10% of those with low trust.

According to recent reports, misconduct and scientific fraud were not included among the reasons Nature’s survey-takers could select as drivers of falling public trust — an omission of the survey design, in hindsight. But in free-text answers, some respondents remarked that they felt scientists were partly to blame for public opinion turning against them. One social scientist in the United States wrote that “rampant fraud” in research, such as fabricated data and scientists racing to publish as much as possible with scant thought to the value of their research, has rightly drained public trust. He says that he feels “furious” that academics have undermined their own credibility. “I literally am embarrassed to tell people in my community what I do for a living,” he writes.

In a recent development, another US respondent, an engineering researcher who noted he comes from a cattle ranching family in Texas, wrote that academia “has earned every bit of scepticism that it receives from the public”. Most scientists don’t understand working-class people, he wrote. “When we use the degrees we earned at protected bubbles on university campuses to say that ‘we know best, give us power’, we have to accept that we are nearly always wrong.”.

Astronomers witness a star eating its companion in 1st-of-its-kind observation

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (643 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Astronomers may have, for the first time ever, directly witnessed a star engulfing its companion, a latest study reports.
  • Industry observers note that as stars die, they swell up to hundreds of times their original size, consuming anything orbiting nearby.
  • "Catching a star engulfing its companion in the act is very difficult," study lead author Viraj Karambelkar, an astrophysicist at Columbia University in Fresh York, told Space.com.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Astronomers may have, for the first time ever, directly witnessed a star engulfing its companion, a latest study reports.

Industry observers note that as stars die, they swell up to hundreds of times their original size, consuming anything orbiting nearby. In a binary star system, this can include a dying star merging with its companion star. However, scientists had never directly seen any examples of such a cosmic drama unfolding — until now.

"Catching a star engulfing its companion in the act is very difficult," study lead author Viraj Karambelkar, an astrophysicist at Columbia University in Fresh York, told Space.com. "When a star engulfs its companion, its effect is very subtle — like throwing a bucket of water in a large ocean. We need sensitive telescopes monitoring the sky for a long time in order to catch this effect.".

In a recent development, in the fresh study, the researchers investigated a red giant star designated WNTR23bzdiq, which is located about 2.5 million light-years away in the Andromeda galaxy. The star is about seven times heftier and 350 times wider than our own sun.

Recent findings suggest that in 2023, using NASA's now-defunct NEOWISE space telescope and the WINTER telescope at Palomar Observatory in California, the scientists noticed that this star was brightening. By analyzing previous records, they found that the red giant had gradually started growing more luminous in 2018.

The researchers had previously suggested this brightening potentially occurred because the giant star engulfed a companion star. As this companion spiraled toward the giant's core, it would generate friction, heat and light, explaining the increasing luminosity.

Then, near the end of 2025, the astronomers saw a giant eruption of light from this giant star. NASA's James Webb Space Telescope observed the star just 47 days after that eruption, allowing the team to characterize the event in detail. The researchers now propose that this explosion happened when a companion star about 70% the sun's mass rammed into the giant's heart.

"I was absolutely flabbergasted when we saw this," Karambelkar noted.

Industry observers note that in the newly introduced study, the scientists estimated that the eruption expelled an amount of material equal to about 0.1 to 0.2 times the mass of the sun. "Stars engulfing their companions have been theorized for many decades, and this event provides the first observations of this theoretical prediction," Karambelkar remarked.

According to recent reports, although these findings suggest that two stars — a binary system nicknamed "Bao" — merged into one, "it is not the only possibility," Karambelkar stated. "The other possibility is that both stars survived, in a much shorter orbit. In order to conclusively determine what happened, we need to continue monitoring what the system does, once the heft of the eruption settles down.".

It has been revealed that now that astronomers may have found the first such merger, "I can't wait to find more," Karambelkar said. "Upcoming telescopes like the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope and the Vera Rubin Observatory will be very useful in discovering many more such events.".

According to recent reports, the scientists detailed their findings Nov. 18 in the journal Nature.
